note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Assist in the provision of on the job training

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: At a fabrication shop in Old Harbour, a senior welder is asked to help train a new apprentice on the job. What is his main duty in this role?
options: To do the apprentice's welds for him when time is short
To guide him to work safely and to the standard
To sign the apprentice off as competent for the NVQ-J
To keep the apprentice on cleaning duties for a year

questions.stem: Where does the role of a welder who assists with on-the-job training normally stop?
options: He coaches and reports; a qualified assessor judges competence
He sets the apprentice's rate of pay once the training is complete
He writes the national standard for the apprentice's trade
He prints and issues the apprentice's final certificate

questions.stem: An experienced welder on your team chips slag without safety glasses while the apprentices watch. Why does this matter for their training?
options: It does not matter, as apprentices learn mostly from the manuals
It only matters if the shop is being audited that day
It matters only for welders with less than a year's work
Apprentices copy what they see, so they learn the unsafe habit

questions.stem: Tevin, a new helper, says he 'did some welding at school'. What is the best way to find out what he can really do?
options: Put him straight on to a 6G pipe test
Take his word for it and give him production work at once
Watch him set up and run beads on scrap plate
Give him a written quiz on welding history

questions.stem: Which document best sets out what an apprentice welder must be able to do for the qualification?
options: The shop's price list for welding jobs
The unit standards for the qualification
The welding machine's spare parts list
The supplier's catalogue of electrodes and wire

questions.stem: An apprentice makes sound flat fillet welds, but his vertical-up welds sag and show undercut. What should his next training focus on?
options: More flat fillet welds until every one of them is perfect
Gas cutting, to give him a change of task
Reading drawings before any more welding
Vertical-up technique: angle, weave and current

questions.stem: Why should a training needs analysis compare what the apprentice can do now with what the shop's work needs?
options: So the apprentice can be paid for each new skill
So the trainer can leave out the safety induction
So the gap shows which training to plan first
So the shop need not keep any training records

questions.stem: An apprentice is to learn to tack a butt joint. Which objective tells you most clearly what he must be able to do at the end?
options: Tack two 6 mm plates with a 2 mm gap, square and in line, unaided
Understand what tacking is and why welders need to use it on every job
Learn all about butt joints, tack welds and root gaps
Watch the trainer tack a pair of plates together

questions.stem: This month you must train an apprentice in oxy-fuel cutting, MMAW tacking and fillet welding. Which order makes most sense?
options: Fillet welding first, since it is the hardest
Any order, since the skills do not link up
Cutting, then tacking, then fillet welding
All three in one day to get them done

questions.stem: A gate and grille contract starts next month. Why is it a good chance to plan the apprentice's training around it?
options: The client will pay extra for the training hours
He learns on real work, to a real standard
Real jobs do not need trainees to be watched
Faults on real jobs never need putting right

questions.stem: Who should agree the apprentice's training plan with you before you start to use it?
options: The apprentice's parents only
The steel supplier's sales agent
Nobody; the trainer decides alone
The supervisor and the apprentice

questions.stem: You will demonstrate a fillet weld with MMAW tomorrow. Which preparation matters most?
options: Check the booth, machine, leads, PPE, plate and rods
Order a new welding machine for the demonstration
Write a long handout on the history of arc welding for him
Ask the apprentice to bring his own electrodes

questions.stem: Why use clean offcut plate for an apprentice's first practice welds, rather than a customer's job?
options: Offcuts need less current than new plate
Customers never allow apprentices on site
Mistakes cost little and spoil no client's work
Offcuts never need cleaning or grinding before welding

questions.stem: Where is the best place to demonstrate tacking to two apprentices in a busy fabrication shop?
options: On the open floor, right beside the guillotine and the saw
Out in the yard, near the gas cylinder store
In the office, using pictures only
At a screened booth where both can see safely

questions.stem: Before an apprentice strikes his first arc in the shop, what must the trainer be sure of?
options: That he owns a welding machine of his own
That he has the right PPE and knows the hazards
That he can already weld in every position on plate and pipe
That he has read every page of the manual

questions.stem: During a demonstration, two apprentices stand behind you without helmets or screens. Why is this a problem?
options: Arc light can burn unprotected eyes and skin
They will learn the task faster than the others
Onlookers make the arc harder to strike
Only the person welding needs eye protection

questions.stem: An apprentice is welding galvanised pipe for a fence job. Which extra control should the trainer insist on?
options: A lower current so the zinc does not melt
Wetting the pipe first to cool the coating
Working faster to finish before fumes build up
Local fume extraction or a suitable respirator

questions.stem: You are teaching an apprentice to set up an oxy-acetylene cutting set. Which check should he learn to do every time before lighting up?
options: Open the acetylene valve fully to clear it
Grease the regulator threads so they seal
Check hoses, fittings and arrestors for leaks
Light the torch first, then fit the regulators

questions.stem: You are asked to supervise six new apprentices welding at once in a shop with four booths. What should you do?
options: Explain the risk and agree smaller groups
Let them share booths two at a time
Supervise them from the office window
Let the best one supervise the others

questions.stem: Why should a new apprentice be shown, on his first day, where the fire extinguishers, first-aid kit and gas shut-off valves are?
options: So he can refill the extinguishers himself when they are used
So he can act quickly and safely in an emergency
So he can sign the shop's stock records
So he can move the cylinders without asking

questions.stem: An apprentice gets a small spatter burn on his wrist. What is the right first aid?
options: Burst any blister and cover it with grease
Rub ice on it hard for a few seconds
Cool it under cool running water, then report it
Wrap it tightly in tape and carry on welding

questions.stem: Which approach works best when teaching a practical skill such as running a stringer bead?
options: Give a long talk on the theory, then let him try it once
Hand him the rods and let him work it out
Show it once at full speed, then leave him
Explain, show, let him try, then check and correct

questions.stem: While you weld, the apprentice cannot see the weld pool clearly. What is the best way to let him see what you see?
options: Let him watch from beside you, with a helmet on
Let him look at the arc without a filter for a moment
Describe the weld pool afterwards from memory
Show him a photo of a finished weld instead

questions.stem: While demonstrating, why explain the reason for cleaning mill scale and rust off the joint before welding?
options: It makes the trainer look more experienced
Knowing the reason helps him remember and apply it
The client asks for an explanation of each step
It gives the plates time to cool down first

questions.stem: Setting up a MIG (GMAW) set has 14 steps. What is the best way to teach it to a new apprentice?
options: Teach all 14 steps at once, then test him
Give him the maker's manual and leave him to read it alone
Only teach the steps you think really matter
Group the steps into stages and teach each in turn

questions.stem: How can you best confirm that an apprentice really understands how to choose the current for a 3.2 mm electrode?
options: Ask him if he understands and accept a nod
Tell him the setting again, more loudly
Have him set it and explain how he chose it
Give him the setting on a card to keep

questions.stem: The shop is noisy and everyone wears ear defenders. How should you give an apprentice instructions during a task?
options: Shout the instructions over the grinders
Stop the noisy work, then speak face to face
Lift one of his ear defenders while the grinders are running
Wait until the end of the day to tell him

questions.stem: An apprentice struggles to read the written WPS but welds well. How should you help him use the WPS?
options: Go through it with him, using sketches and the real joint
Tell him to skip the WPS since he already welds well
Give him a longer written guide to read at home
Ask another apprentice to weld all his coded jobs

questions.stem: An apprentice calls every weld fault a 'bad weld'. Why is it worth teaching him the proper names, such as porosity and undercut?
options: So he sounds clever when clients visit
So he can avoid being told about his faults by the supervisor
So he can find the cause and report it clearly
So the shop can charge more for his welds

questions.stem: An apprentice welding a practice coupon is holding a very long arc. What should you do?
options: Let him finish, then tell him next week
Take the holder and finish it yourself
Say nothing; he will learn by his mistakes
Stop him, show the right arc length, let him retry

questions.stem: Why should an apprentice weld several practice coupons before a test coupon is taken for assessment?
options: So the skill is steady and right every time
So the shop uses up its old stock of plate
So the assessor has more coupons to choose from
So he gets tired and the test is harder

questions.stem: Your apprentice's 2F fillet weld has the right leg size, but the upper toe shows undercut. What should you tell him?
options: That weld is bad; just do it again
Good size; try a shorter arc and a little less current
Good weld; well done, just keep going
Undercut again; you really should know better than that by now

questions.stem: Why should feedback give one or two clear points to improve, rather than every small fault at once?
options: Trainers may not point out more than two faults
Small faults never matter in welding work
It saves the trainer's time at the end of the day
Too many points at once confuse and discourage

questions.stem: How can a trainer check that an apprentice's practice butt welds are sound inside, not only on the surface?
options: Cut and bend coupons, or etch a cross-section
Look at the weld again from further away
Paint the weld and see if the paint sticks
Tap the weld and listen for a clear ring

questions.stem: Which evidence best shows that an apprentice can now cut plate to a line safely, without close supervision?
options: He says he feels confident with the torch
He has watched you cut many plates
He did it right, unaided, on several jobs
He passed a written test on gas cutting

questions.stem: After three weeks, an apprentice still forgets to close the cylinder valves at the end of the day. What should you do?
options: Close them for him and say nothing
Report it, retrain him and check each day
Ban him from the shop until he remembers
Let him find out what happens if he forgets

questions.stem: Why should a coupon that an apprentice has bent in the vice be photographed and kept with his training records?
options: It is evidence of the standard he has reached
It lets the shop sell the bent coupon later as scrap metal
It proves the vice is working properly
It means no assessor is needed later

questions.stem: Which entry in an apprentice's training record is best?
options: Did some welding this week and it looked OK to me
Kemar is a good worker; trust him with any job
Practised welding all week; still needs more time
3 Nov: 2F fillet, 8 mm plate, to WPS; visual pass; signed

questions.stem: An apprentice is falling behind the agreed plan because the shop keeps putting him on cleaning. What should you do?
options: Say nothing, as cleaning is part of the job
Tell him to train himself in the evenings
Tell the supervisor and agree time for training
Sign off his tasks anyway so that he keeps to the agreed plan

questions.stem: How can you tell whether the training you gave on oxy-fuel cutting has worked?
options: The apprentice said he enjoyed the session
His cuts now meet the standard without help
The session finished on time, as planned
You used all the gas set aside for it

questions.stem: Two apprentices trained by the same method make very different progress. What should the trainer think about first?
options: That the slower one should leave the trade
That the method must be right for everyone
That the faster one has been helped by others
That each may need a different way of learning

questions.stem: A woman apprentice joins the fabrication team, and some workers say heavy work is 'not for her'. What should the trainer do?
options: Give her the same tasks and chances, with lifting aids
Keep her on office work and stores to avoid any trouble on the floor
Let the other workers decide what she may do
Give her only light jobs for the first year

questions.stem: An apprentice must log 120 hours of supervised MMAW practice. He gets 6 hours a week. How many weeks will it take?
options: 12 weeks
18 weeks
20 weeks
26 weeks

questions.stem: Of 8 practice coupons an apprentice bent this month, 6 passed. What is his pass rate?
The shop's rules say apprentices may not use the plasma cutter until they are signed off. An apprentice asks to use it on a rush job. What should you do?
options: Refuse until he is trained and signed off
Let him use it, as the job is urgent and you will be nearby
Let him use it if he wears extra PPE
Let him use it while you go to lunch

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A senior welder is paired with an apprentice for his whole first year, to advise him on the trade and on good work habits. What is the senior welder's role called?
An apprentice needs 160 hours of supervised practice. He gets 8 hours a week. How many weeks will it take?
What name is given to a strip cut from a test weld and bent to check that the weld is sound?
An apprentice bent 12 practice coupons and 9 of them passed. What percentage passed?
An apprentice works 8 hours a day, 5 days a week, and 25% of that time is set aside for training. How many training hours does he get each week?
What document, often known by three letters, sets out the process, consumable, current range and joint preparation for a coded weld?
During feedback, you point to a notch along the edge of the weld where the arc has eaten into the plate and the notch was not filled. What is this fault called?
What is the name for the first session in which a new worker is shown the shop rules, hazards, exits and first-aid points?
A trainer supervises 3 apprentices for 4 hours in the morning and 2 apprentices for 3 hours in the afternoon. How many apprentice-hours of supervised training is that?
When you teach an apprentice to check a gas set for leaks, what is brushed onto the joints so that a leak shows up as bubbles?
What is the name of the qualified person who makes the formal judgement of a trainee's competence against the standard?
What name is given to the collection of evidence, such as photos, signed tasks and test coupons, that shows a trainee's competence?
What is the learning style of a trainee who learns best by hearing explanations and talking things through?
What is the name of the formal period, under an agreement with an employer, in which a young person learns a trade while working?
What one-word name is given to the check made by eye on a finished weld for its size, shape and surface faults?

essays.stem: A shop owner asks you, a Level 3 welder, to 'take the new apprentices under your wing'. Explain what your duties as an on-the-job trainer would be, who else shares the training, and what you must leave to others.
essays.modelAnswer: The welder who assists with on-the-job training guides apprentices so they learn to work safely and to the shop's standard. He helps find out what each apprentice can already do, plans training around real jobs with the supervisor, prepares the booth, plate and PPE, demonstrates tasks, watches practice closely and corrects faults at once. He gives clear feedback, checks progress against the unit standards and keeps the logbook or training record up to date. He sets a good example, because apprentices copy what they see. Others are involved too: the supervisor agrees the plan and gives time for training, the training officer or the Centre keeps the programme on track, and a qualified assessor makes the formal judgement of competence. The trainer's role ends at reporting progress and evidence; he does not sign anyone off as competent for the qualification himself.
markingPoints: Guides apprentices to work safely and to the standard
Plans, prepares, demonstrates, supervises practice and gives feedback
Checks progress and keeps the training record
Names others involved: supervisor, training officer, assessor
Role ends at reporting; the assessor judges competence

essays.stem: Shanique has just started as an apprentice at a fabrication shop in Spanish Town. Explain the steps you would take to discover her present skills and the gaps she must close.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would talk with Shanique about her schooling, any welding or metalwork she has done and what she wants to learn, and look at any certificates. Then I would watch her do simple tasks safely on scrap: set up a booth, strike an arc and run beads, mark out and cut a plate, and use a grinder with the guard on. I would ask her to explain the steps and the hazards, to check her understanding. I would compare what I saw with the unit standards for the qualification and with the work the shop does, such as gates, grilles and frames. The difference is her training need. I would list the gaps in order, safety first, then the basic skills that later skills build on. I would agree the list with her and the supervisor, and record it so progress can be measured later.
markingPoints: Talks with her about past experience and goals
Watches her do real tasks safely on scrap and asks questions
Compares with the unit standards and the shop's work to find the gap
Puts the gaps in order, safety and basic skills first
Agrees and records the needs with her and the supervisor

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan a training session to teach an apprentice to set up, light, use and shut down an oxy-acetylene cutting set.
essays.modelAnswer: I would write a clear objective: by the end, the apprentice will set up, leak test, light, cut a straight line in 10 mm plate and shut down the set safely, without help. I would book a cutting bay away from other work, with the cylinders chained upright, and check the regulators, hoses, flashback arrestors and torch before the session. I would have PPE ready: gas goggles or a face shield of a suitable shade, gloves, jacket and boots, and a fire extinguisher at hand. The steps would be broken into stages: fitting and checking, leak testing with leak detection solution, setting pressures as the maker's chart says, lighting and setting a neutral flame, cutting, and shutting down and bleeding the lines. I would plan time to demonstrate, then for the apprentice to practise each stage with me watching, and end with questions, feedback and a record in his logbook.
markingPoints: Clear, measurable objective
Safe area and equipment checked before the session (cylinders, hoses, arrestors)
PPE and fire precautions ready
Task broken into stages in the right order, including leak test and shut-down
Time for demonstration, supervised practice, feedback and recording

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would teach an apprentice to make a horizontal fillet weld (2F) with MMAW, from the first explanation to checking his finished coupon.
essays.modelAnswer: Explain: in a quiet, screened booth I would tell the apprentice what we will make, why a fillet weld is used, and the key points: clean plates, tack square, current in the maker's range, a short arc, the electrode at about 45 degrees between the plates and slightly in the direction of travel. Demonstrate: with his helmet on and standing beside me, he watches me tack and weld a short run, while I name each step. I then show it again, pausing to point out the weld pool and how I keep the legs even. Practise: he welds his own coupon while I watch closely and stop him at once if anything is unsafe or the arc is too long. He repeats until the welds are steady. Check: we inspect the weld together with a fillet gauge for leg size, undercut and shape, I ask him why each step matters, and I record the result.
markingPoints: Explains the task and key points before starting
Demonstrates safely, with the apprentice protected and able to see
Supervised practice with corrections, repeated until steady
Checks the weld with a gauge and checks understanding with questions
Records the result

essays.stem: List and explain the controls you would put in place so that apprentices learning on the floor of a working fabrication shop are not harmed.
essays.modelAnswer: Before anything else, each apprentice gets a shop induction: exits, extinguishers, first aid, gas shut-offs and the rules. I check their PPE fits and is in good condition: helmet with the right shade, safety glasses, gloves, jacket, boots and ear protection. They only weld in screened booths, so others are not exposed to arc light, and they only use machines such as grinders, shears and plasma cutters after training and sign-off. I keep the group small so I can watch each one, and I never leave a new apprentice alone on a hazardous task. I make sure there is fume extraction, especially for galvanised or painted steel. I teach them to treat all metal as hot, to keep gas cylinders upright and chained, and to clear anything that can burn. If I see an unsafe act I stop the work at once, explain why, and show the safe way.
markingPoints: Induction covering emergency points and rules
Correct PPE checked and worn
Screens, fume extraction and fire precautions
Machines used only after training and sign-off; small groups, close supervision
Unsafe acts stopped at once and corrected

essays.stem: An apprentice's practice welds keep showing porosity, even after a week of practice. Explain how you would find the cause and coach him to put it right.
essays.modelAnswer: I would not just tell him to try harder. I would watch him weld from start to finish and check the likely causes one by one. Are the plates clean and dry, free of rust, oil and paint? Are the electrodes damp, or low-hydrogen rods left out of the oven? Is the arc too long, or is he welding in a draught that blows the shielding away? If he uses MIG, is the gas flow right, is the nozzle clean and is the hose leaking? I would ask him what he thinks the cause is, to make him think it through. When we find the cause, I would explain why it makes porosity, show the correct method, and have him weld new coupons while I watch. We would break or cut a coupon to check inside. I would record the problem and the progress in his logbook.
markingPoints: Watches the whole process rather than guessing
Checks likely causes: dirty plate, damp electrodes, long arc, draught, gas flow
Involves the apprentice in finding the cause
Explains, demonstrates the fix and supervises new practice
Checks the result (cut or break) and records progress

essays.stem: An apprentice has just welded a practice tee joint with uneven legs and a lot of spatter. Set out how you would give him feedback, and say why each part of your approach matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I would give the feedback soon after the weld, in a quiet spot away from the grinders, and make it a two-way talk. First I would ask him how he thinks it went, because he learns more if he spots faults himself. Then we would look at the weld together with a fillet gauge. I would start with what was good, for example a straight bead and a well-filled start, so he keeps doing it. Then I would give one or two clear points: 'The bottom leg is about 8 mm and the top only 5 mm, so point the rod evenly between the plates at about 45 degrees. The spatter tells me the arc is long and the current may be high, so shorten the arc and check the setting.' Clear, specific points are easier to act on than 'bad weld'. I would ask him to say back what he will change, watch his next coupon and record the result.
markingPoints: Given soon after, privately, as a two-way talk
Starts by asking him and naming what was done well
One or two specific points with cause and fix (angle for uneven legs; arc length or current for spatter)
Avoids vague or belittling words
Checks understanding, follows up on the next coupon and records it

essays.stem: Your supervisor asks whether an apprentice is ready to weld 3G butt joints on customer work without you standing beside him. Explain how you would decide, and what evidence you would record.
essays.modelAnswer: I would compare his work with the standard for the task: the WPS and the unit standard. I would watch him do the whole job on his own, more than once, from preparing and tacking the plates to cleaning up, without me helping. I would check that he works safely every time, sets the machine within the WPS range and controls the weld in the vertical position. The finished welds would be checked by eye for size, profile and surface faults, and test coupons would be cut and bent, or sectioned, to check inside. I would ask him why each step matters. If all is right on each attempt, I would report to the supervisor that he can work with less supervision. I would record the date, the task, the WPS, the results of the visual and bend tests, any points still to improve, and both our signatures, with photos of the coupons.
markingPoints: Uses the standard (WPS, unit standard) as the yardstick
Watches him work unaided, more than once, safely
Checks results: visual inspection plus bend or section tests
Asks questions to check understanding; reports to the supervisor
Records date, task, results, points to improve, signatures and photos

essays.stem: An apprentice has taken the guard off an angle grinder because he says it 'gets in the way'. Explain what you would do and why.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stop him at once and have him switch off and unplug the grinder. A grinder without its guard is very dangerous: if the disc bursts, pieces fly out at high speed and can cause serious injury, and the guard also stops the hand touching the disc. I would explain this calmly, then refit the guard myself in front of him, set at the right angle, and check the disc is the right size and rated for the grinder's speed. Then I would show him how to hold the grinder and position the guard so it does not get in the way of the job. I would have him work again while I watch. Because removing a guard is a serious breach, I would record it and tell the supervisor, and if it happens again it would be handled under the shop's rules. I would also check whether other apprentices have picked up the same habit.
markingPoints: Stops the work at once, switches off and isolates
Explains the danger of a missing guard (bursting disc, contact)
Refits the guard and checks the disc rating
Shows the correct method and supervises practice
Records and reports the breach; checks others

essays.stem: Three months after you began training two apprentices, the shop owner asks whether the training has been worth the time. Explain how you would gather the evidence and report back.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the objectives in the training plan and check each one. The main evidence is the apprentice's work: are his welds now passing visual inspection and bend tests, can he do the tasks unaided, and does he work safely every time? I would compare his first records with his latest ones to show the progress, for example his bend test pass rate rising from 50% to 90%. I would ask the apprentice what helped him learn and what did not, and ask the supervisor and other welders how he works on real jobs. I would also look at time and cost: were the sessions done as planned, or did production pressure push them aside? I would write a short report to the supervisor with the results, the gaps still left, and suggestions, such as more vertical practice or fewer apprentices per trainer. The next training plan would be changed to use these lessons.
markingPoints: Checks results against the plan's objectives
Uses evidence from the work: tests, unaided tasks, safety
Compares early and later records to show progress
Asks the apprentice and supervisor for their views
Writes a short report and uses it to improve the next plan

practical1.title: Plan, demonstrate and coach a horizontal fillet weld (2F), with a session plan and feedback records
practical1.brief: Your group is the training team in a fabrication shop. Together, write a one-page session plan for teaching a new apprentice to make a two-pass horizontal fillet weld (2F) on a tee joint with MMAW: the objective, the steps, the key points, the safety points and how the result will be checked. Then share the session into five stages: (1) safety briefing and booth check, (2) machine set-up and current setting, (3) tacking the tee joint, (4) welding the fillet, (5) inspecting the weld and giving feedback. Each member is the trainer for at least one stage and the trainee for another, so every member both teaches and welds. The trainer explains, demonstrates, watches the trainee practise and gives feedback; the trainee then explains the step back. Each trainer fills in a feedback form for the trainee they coached. Photograph each stage. Hand in the session plan, the welded coupons and the feedback forms once for the whole group.
materials: MMAW machines in screened booths, with leads, electrode holders and work clamps
8–10 mm carbon steel plate offcuts, about 150 mm × 75 mm, two per member
3.2 mm E6013 electrodes (or as the Centre's WPS says)
Chipping hammers, wire brushes and an angle grinder for cleaning
Session plan template, feedback forms and logbook pages
Full welding PPE for every member
photos: The written session plan, with each member's stage named
The safety briefing and booth check, with all members in PPE
A trainer demonstrating tacking while the trainee watches with a helmet on
A trainee welding the fillet while the trainer watches beside him
The finished coupons, with the fillet gauge on each weld
The completed feedback forms laid out
The booths cleaned, stubs in a metal container
checklist: Helped write a session plan with a clear, measurable objective and ordered steps
As trainer, explained the stage in plain words and named the key points and hazards
As trainer, gave a safe demonstration that the trainee could see with eye protection
As trainer, watched the practice closely and stepped in at once on any unsafe act or fault
As trainer, checked understanding by asking the trainee to explain or show the step
As trainer, gave specific feedback (one good point, one or two to improve) and filled in the form
As trainee, welded a sound coupon to the gauge size, working safely
Wore full PPE and left the booth safe and tidy
safety: Weld only in screened booths; everyone watching wears a helmet or stands behind a screen
Check leads, holders and clamps before use; keep gloves dry
Treat all metal as hot; use tongs and mark hot coupons
Keep the area clear of anything that can burn, with an extinguisher at hand
Keep fumes away from the face; use the extraction

practical2.title: Skills check on oxy-fuel cutting, a two-week training plan and a progress review role play
practical2.brief: Your group will act as the workplace trainers for a new apprentice. Part 1: in pairs, each member carries out a structured skills check on another member, who sets up an oxy-acetylene cutting set, leak tests it, lights it, cuts a straight line along a marked line in 10 mm plate and shuts the set down. The checker uses the group's skills checklist and writes down what was done well and any gaps. Every member is checked once and checks once. Part 2: using the apprentice profile the assessor gives you, the group writes a two-week on-the-job training plan for that apprentice: the needs found, the objectives, the tasks in order, who trains each one, the time, the safety points and how progress will be checked. Part 3: two members role play a progress review between the trainer and the apprentice at the end of week one, using the plan; the others observe and complete the review record. Photograph each part.
materials: Oxy-acetylene cutting sets with regulators, flashback arrestors and hoses in good condition, cylinders chained upright
10 mm carbon steel plate, about 300 mm × 150 mm, with a marked line, one per member
Spark lighter, tip cleaners, square, scriber and soapstone
Gas cutting goggles or face shield of a suitable shade, gloves, jacket and boots for every member
Skills checklist, apprentice profile (from the assessor), training plan and review record templates
photos: The cutting set checked and leak tested, with the solution on the joints
A member cutting along the line while the checker watches with the checklist
The cut plates laid out, each labelled with the member's name
The progress review role play, with the review record being filled in
checklist: Checked the set before use: cylinders secure, hoses, regulators and flashback arrestors, leak test with solution
Lit, set a neutral flame, cut along the line and shut down in the correct order
As checker, used the checklist fairly and wrote clear, specific notes
Helped turn the gaps into objectives and tasks in a sensible order
The training plan names times, trainers, safety points and how progress is checked
Took part in the review: discussed progress, agreed next steps, recorded them
Worked safely and kept the cutting area clear of anything that can burn
safety: Cylinders upright and chained; open valves slowly and never use oil or grease on oxygen fittings
Leak test with solution, never with a flame
Cut over a cutting table or sand, with anything that can burn cleared away and an extinguisher at hand
Wear goggles or a face shield of a suitable shade; treat all cut plate and slag as hot
Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothing; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
